sections.heading: What Makes SVG Different From Other Image Formats
paragraphs: SVG stores shapes as mathematical descriptions rather than a fixed grid of colored dots. This is why it can scale to any size without losing quality, while a PNG becomes pixelated when enlarged.
The trade-off is that SVG requires software capable of interpreting vector math, which is why email clients, older systems and many publishing services demand a raster version.
PNG offers lossless compression, making it ideal for logos and graphics with sharp edges, flat colors and transparency.
Rasterizing an SVG preserves the visual design exactly while converting its infinite geometry into a bounded, universally compatible pixel grid.

sections.heading: Picking the Right PNG Size for the Job
paragraphs: The ideal output size depends on the destination: an app icon needs only a few hundred pixels, while a poster or banner demands export at thousands of pixels.
Exporting at two times the needed display size gives crisp results on retina and high-density screens, and the SVGs redraw cleanly to supply those extra pixels.
For print, match the output dimensions to the physical size and print resolution, typically 300 dots per inch.
Starting from the vector guarantees that any of these sizes stays sharp, because the conversion always re-renders from the original geometry.
